Annuity guarantee periods: distinguish lifetime payments from a fixed payment term

Compare original life-annuity and term-certain payment calendars, follow recipients after an assumed death, and inspect remaining guaranteed instalments in four interactive figures.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare two invented annuity payment calendars and their recipient rules

Interactive planning lab

Life annuity: all recipients’ payments within the window$122,400
Term-certain annuity: all recipients’ payments within the window$72,000
Full guaranteed instalments remaining after the assumed death$0

Two original contract-calendar illustrations share an independently selected annual payment. This does not imply equal purchase premiums, equivalent value, an available quote or an appropriate product choice. Contract A pays for the annuitant’s life, with a guaranteed minimum payment period; if death occurs earlier, a beneficiary receives remaining scheduled guarantee payments. Contract B pays only for that fixed term, with remaining instalments directed to a beneficiary after an earlier death. Payment one occurs at the end of year one; death is assumed immediately after the selected year’s payment. No mortality probabilities or life-expectancy estimates are used. Totals include only the chosen display window, whereas the full remaining-guarantee metric refers to the entire schedule after the assumed death and may extend beyond the window. It is not an immediate lump sum, account balance or additional money to add to already counted receipts. Payments are undiscounted and before tax; purchase prices, inflation, discounting, commutation, cashback, joint-survivor benefits, fees, surrender values and insurer-default protection are not calculated.

The central idea

A minimum guaranteed period can protect payments after an early death without placing an end date on life-contingent income. A fixed-term contract has a different stopping rule.

01

Identify what the contract’s period actually controls

The words “ten years” can describe different annuity features. They might identify a fixed payment term, after which the scheduled income ends. They might instead identify a minimum guaranteed payment period inside a contract that continues paying while the annuitant remains alive.

The distinction affects a retirement cash calendar. Reading only the number of years can conceal either an income stream that stops while someone is still alive or beneficiary payments that continue after an early death.

FCAC’s annuity guide distinguishes lifetime income, fixed-term income and options that continue payments after death. This article applies those general distinctions to two independently specified calendars. It does not reproduce the source’s numerical examples or price either contract.

The default annual payment is CAD 7,200 in each illustration. Matching that amount makes their timing rules easy to inspect; it does not imply that the contracts cost the same premium. Their economic value cannot be ranked from these receipt totals alone.

02

Write down the two stopping rules before counting payments

Contract A is a life annuity with a ten-year minimum payment period. While the annuitant is alive, the assumed CAD 7,200 annual payment continues. If death occurs before all ten guaranteed payments have been made, the remaining scheduled payments go to a beneficiary.

Contract B is a ten-year term-certain annuity. It makes ten annual payments in total. If the annuitant dies before the term ends, the beneficiary receives the remaining instalments; if the annuitant survives the term, the payment still stops after year ten.

Both examples pay at each year-end, starting with year one. The death control means death immediately after the payment in the selected year. This convention assigns that year’s payment to the annuitant and makes any beneficiary payments start in the following year.

Real contracts can use monthly payments, different start dates and different beneficiary settlement terms. Those terms need their own reading. This example assumes continued scheduled instalments and does not convert them into a lump-sum settlement.

03

See what happens when the annuitant lives beyond the guarantee period

The default assumes death after the year-seventeen payment and displays twenty-five contract years. Contract A pays the annuitant for seventeen years, producing 17 × CAD 7,200 = CAD 122,400 of scheduled receipts.

The ten-year guarantee expires during that lifetime. Its expiry does not stop the life-contingent payments in this example. Years eleven through seventeen still pay CAD 7,200 annually. Payments stop after the assumed death because no guaranteed instalments remain.

Contract B pays only through year ten, giving 10 × CAD 7,200 = CAD 72,000. The annuitant is still assumed alive in years eleven through seventeen, but that does not extend the fixed term.

The annual checkpoint bars include the guarantee end, the next year, the assumed death and the following year when those dates are inside the display window. They show payment in each selected year, rather than a cumulative account balance.

04

Move the assumed death earlier and follow the recipient

Change the death year to seven while retaining the ten-year period. The annuitant receives seven payments totaling CAD 50,400. Three guaranteed instalments remain, scheduled for years eight, nine and ten.

Those remaining payments total CAD 21,600 and go to the beneficiary under the chosen rules. The combined scheduled total is CAD 72,000 in either example because death occurred inside their common ten-year minimum schedule.

The recipient bars divide those receipts between annuitant and beneficiary. They do not pay CAD 21,600 twice or add a second benefit beside the ten existing instalments. If the selected death is exactly after year ten’s payment, the remaining guaranteed amount is zero.

The guarantee described here concerns a number of scheduled payments. It is not a promise to refund an unspecified original premium. No purchase premium is entered, and no cash-refund rider or separate survivor’s lifetime income is assumed.

05

Keep the displayed window separate from the full remaining schedule

The cumulative chart adds scheduled receipts at each year-end. It begins at zero because the graph tracks payments received after the contract starts. It does not plot a premium that remains available for withdrawal.

Reducing the display window to eight years in the early-death example includes seven annuitant payments and only the first beneficiary payment. The two cumulative endpoints are then CAD 57,600, with CAD 7,200 of beneficiary receipts included in each endpoint.

The separate remaining-guarantee metric still reports the full CAD 21,600 scheduled after the assumed year-seven death. Two of those instalments lie beyond the shortened display. Adding that metric to the cumulative endpoint would count one payment twice and combine different dates without explanation.

Increasing the window to twenty-five years includes all three beneficiary instalments. A longer chart does not create additional receipts after either contract’s entitlement has ended. Conversely, stopping the graph early does not cancel payments outside its window.

06

Use the matrix as a conditional schedule, not a product quote

Each matrix cell holds the selected annual payment constant and changes the guaranteed period and assumed death year. The remaining instalment count is the positive part of guaranteed years minus completed payment years at death.

For a fifteen-year period and death after year seven, eight payments remain. At CAD 7,200 per year their undiscounted sum is CAD 57,600. If death follows the period’s final payment, the result is zero.

Those totals are not mortality-weighted expected benefits. The model assigns no probability to an early or late death. It also does not discount future payments or calculate the amount an insurer would offer to commute them into a current lump sum.

Changing a guarantee period while holding annual payment fixed is a teaching comparison. Actual pricing can change with contract features and individual circumstances. Obtain the actual premium, payment quote and settlement terms before comparing available contracts.

07

Bring each payment back to its recipient and intended expense

A retirement plan needs to identify whose expenses a payment funds, how long it can continue and what happens at a death. Beneficiary receipts after one person dies may serve a different purpose from the income that person needed while alive.

The displayed dollars are gross receipts before tax, with no assumed spending or reinvestment. They are not profit, remaining capital, an accessible savings balance or a complete measure of household wealth. Purchase costs and alternative uses of that money are deliberately absent.

The illustration also omits inflation indexing, joint-survivor coverage, administrative delays and insurer-default protection. It cannot establish a sufficient retirement budget or the suitability of buying an annuity.

For an actual contract, record the first payment date, frequency, lifetime or term condition, guaranteed-payment wording, beneficiary instructions and any commutation provision. Then use the confirmed schedule alongside the household’s other receipts and obligations. A clear payment calendar makes the meaning of the guarantee visible without assuming that one period describes every feature.
